source.title: Factorized Representations of Concurrent Temporal Variables in Pretrained Language Models

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures overlapping and factorized representations of controlled temporal variables in pretrained language models. It does not test sparse features competing for capacity, polysemanticity, neuron-level feature spread, SAE feature completeness, or superposition of 1-D features as specified by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper studies two experimentally defined event-recency timers, not sparse model features or feature-capacity competition. Its timer subspaces and geometry are relevant adjacent findings, so they are recorded with versions ["none"]. Its mention of in-context superposition is related-work context, not a test of that claim.
record.test_reason: The study measures how two controlled event-recency timers share and separate subspaces in pretrained LMs, using centroid planes, ablation and additivity. It does not measure sparse features versus dimensions, polysemantic neurons, capacity competition, feature spread across neurons, SAE or dictionary features, or whether superposed features are 1-D. Superposition appears only in a cited title (Xiong et al., 'In-context superposition'). The rank-2 timer plane is forced by having three centroids. The horizon sweep's rank is a 90%-variance cut on timer centroids, not a test of feature dimensionality. So V6 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude there is approximate factorization (selective accessibility plus approximately additive joint geometry) within overlapping, nonorthogonal subspaces. It persists across 3–51 timer values and Qwen3 0.6B–14B. Decoded-state interventions do not yield timer-specific output changes.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses controlled event-recency schedules, centroid-derived timer subspaces, linear decoding and subspace ablation in pretrained language models. It does not use the original toy-model feature-sparsity and superposition setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Cross-ablation increases with timer horizon (from 0.15% at H=2 to 4.86% at H=50); the paper also reports that whitening within-class scatter reduces plane alignment and cross-timer decoding.

fits_no_version.finding: Two concurrent timers are linearly decodable from the same middle-layer states. Each timer's centroid plane removes far more of its own signal (84%/57%) than of the other timer's (1.6%/2.8%), although the planes are nonorthogonal (53.9° vs 79.7° for unrelated planes) and share information. Joint centroids are mostly additive (interaction 10.1% vs 5.2% additive floor). Selectivity weakens slowly with horizon. Centroid displacements change decoded state but not continuation outputs in a timer-specific way.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Independently evolving contextual variables in pretrained LMs occupy overlapping, nonorthogonal but selectively accessible subspaces with approximately additive joint geometry.

record.problems: The primary timer corpus is controlled and built from a hand-written bank of propositions. The topic signal is substantially weaker than the language signal. The tested output intervention shows no consistent timer-specific continuation effect. Some reported aggregate results do not state uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted to meet the 60-row limit. Detailed per-model restricted-decoding values and additional appendix analyses are not separately enumerated here.

untested.parts: All of it: no toy networks, no sparse features exceeding dimensions, no sparsity transition or superposition geometry.
All of it: no neurons, polysemanticity, feature importance or capacity competition.
All of it: the causes of polysemanticity are not studied.
All of it: no neuron-level spread and no SAE or dictionary recovery. Timer information is probed in PCA subspaces.
All of it: no dictionary features.
Whether superposed features are 1-D or multi-dimensional. The timer-centroid rank is set by the number of class values and a 90%-variance criterion, not by a feature analysis.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only': superposition appears only in a reference title, and the paper does not discuss the superposition hypothesis. Cross-ablation rows were relabelled 'absent' so their state consistently means 'no effect from concurrent-plane removal'; the reader had mixed 'partial' and 'observed' for near-identical changes. Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B are post-trained checkpoints; the record lists them as 'pretrained'. The study is not an original source. No verdict labels are given because no version is tested.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, sparse features, feature-to-dimension overload, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular superposition geometry are tested.
No polysemantic neurons, feature importance, dedicated dimensions, or capacity competition are measured.
The study does not investigate causes of polysemanticity or whether it is evidence of superposition.
The study does not measure feature spread across neurons or recover sparse features with a dictionary or SAE. It measures controlled timer information in hidden-state subspaces.
No dictionary or SAE features are studied, and completeness, stability, or canonical status of feature units is not assessed.
The rank of timer-associated centroid subspaces is measured, but the study does not identify superposed model features or test whether those features are 1-D or multidimensional.

relation.reason: Section 6.2 cites in-context superposition as related working-memory research; the experiments neither test nor use the catalog's superposition claims.

tranche.reason: The study measures timer accessibility, subspace overlap and additive centroid geometry, without testing capacity-driven superposition, neuron-level feature distribution, dictionary units or irreducibly multidimensional features.

source_check.notes: All 20 sampled rows match the text. The conclusion about output intervention is limited to no consistent timer-specific continuation effect from the tested language-timer displacement from value 1 to value 2.
